actions.name: Review discharge summary and planned services
actions.result: Discharge summary (4 days ago) for AECOPD, 3rd admission this year. Plan: fluticasone/umeclidinium/vilanterol (Trelegy Ellipta) 1 inh daily, prednisone taper (days 1-3: 40mg; days 4-6: 30mg; days 7-9: 20mg; day 10: 10mg, then stop), home O2 2L/min NC, home health nursing eval within 48h of discharge, pulmonology follow-up in 7 days, portable O2 tanks for ambulation/appointments ordered via DME.

actions.name: Reconcile current medications against discharge list
actions.result: Patient confirms she is using old albuterol HFA inhaler (prior prescription, partially full) instead of new Trelegy; prednisone 40mg tablets being taken intermittently (she reports every other day instead of daily per taper) rather than the prescribed daily taper.

actions.name: Ask patient to read current pulse oximeter reading at rest
actions.result: Home pulse oximeter: SpO2 91% on 2L supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula, heart rate 94 bpm, patient reports mild breathlessness while reading numbers aloud, no accessory muscle use visible on camera.

actions.name: Ask patient to count respiratory rate for 30 seconds via camera
actions.result: Respiratory rate 22/min, slightly labored but able to complete full sentences.

actions.name: Screen for red-flag respiratory symptoms (worsening SOB, fever, change in sputum, chest pain, confusion)
actions.result: No fever, no chest pain, no confusion. Sputum unchanged in color (white/clear). Reports breathlessness is same as at discharge, not acutely worse.

actions.name: Assess home oxygen equipment and ambulatory oxygen access
actions.result: Stationary concentrator delivering 2L/min confirmed in home; patient states no portable tanks or portable concentrator have arrived; has not left apartment since discharge.

actions.name: Assess fall/mobility risk in home environment (stairs, bathroom)
actions.result: Patient lives in second-floor walk-up with no elevator; reports shortness of breath climbing the stairs even before this admission; bathroom has no grab bars.

actions.name: Assess medication cost/insurance barriers
actions.result: Patient reports $95 copay quoted at pharmacy for Trelegy Ellipta; has Medicare Part D plan with no additional low-income subsidy or supplemental assistance; did not pick up medication due to cost.

actions.name: Assess transportation access for pulmonology follow-up
actions.result: Patient no longer drives (stopped 2 years ago); pulmonology clinic is across town; no established medical transport; daughter is out of state and cannot drive her.

actions.name: Assess home health nursing contact status
actions.result: Home health referral was placed at discharge; patient reports no call or visit received in 4 days since discharge.

actions.name: Screen for caregiver support and social isolation
actions.result: Daughter lives in Texas, calls daily by phone but cannot provide in-person help; patient lives alone; no local family or paid caregiver identified; neighbor sometimes checks in.

actions.name: Assess food and nutrition access during recovery
actions.result: Patient reports she has enough groceries for about a week delivered by a neighbor; no immediate food insecurity identified at this time.

actions.name: Document findings and gaps in case management assessment note
actions.result: Case management note documents: medication non-adherence due to cost and symptom (insomnia from prednisone), missing portable oxygen delaying DME order completion, home health referral not actioned, transportation barrier to pulmonology follow-up, SpO2 91% on 2L with mild tachypnea, no acute red flags at this time.

actions.name: Place/escalate urgent order for portable oxygen and confirm DME follow-up
actions.result: Order placed with DME vendor flagged urgent; vendor confirms portable tank delivery can be expedited within 24-48 hours; case manager documents escalation and sets follow-up call to confirm delivery.

actions.name: Submit urgent re-referral to home health agency with reason for delay
actions.result: Re-referral submitted to home health agency noting no contact made within required 48-hour window; agency confirms will prioritize visit within 24 hours and will notify case manager once scheduled.

actions.name: Document medication affordability barrier and initiate pharmacy assistance referral
actions.result: Case manager documents $95 copay barrier for Trelegy Ellipta and initiates referral to pharmacy financial assistance program/manufacturer copay support and screening for Medicare Extra Help (Low-Income Subsidy); flags pulmonology team that patient has been using old albuterol only in the interim.

actions.name: Arrange non-emergency medical transportation for pulmonology follow-up
actions.result: Case manager arranges Medicare-covered non-emergency medical transportation (NEMT) pickup for the scheduled pulmonology visit; confirms address, mobility needs (oxygen tank in transit), and appointment time with transport vendor.

actions.name: Set and document escalation/red-flag instructions with patient and daughter
actions.result: Case manager reviews specific red-flag symptoms (SpO2 persistently <88% off supplemental O2 target range, worsening breathlessness at rest, confusion, fever, chest pain, inability to speak full sentences) warranting call to pulmonology or 911; confirms patient and daughter both understand plan; documents teach-back completed.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Post-discharge care transition breakdown after third COPD exacerbation admission this year: multiple unaddressed barriers (medication cost non-adherence, missing portable oxygen, absent home health follow-up, and transportation gap) placing patient at high risk for readmission.
differential: Medication non-adherence from cost barrier (Trelegy copay) rather than refusal
Prednisone under-dosing from symptom-driven self-rationing (insomnia) rather than noncompliance with understanding
Early/evolving re-exacerbation vs. stable but under-resourced recovery
Social isolation/caregiver strain contributing to risk, not causing it
keyFindings: SpO2 91% on 2L oxygen with mild tachypnea (RR 22) and reported baseline-level breathlessness, no acute red flags
No portable oxygen tanks delivered; patient homebound since discharge
Home health nursing never made contact despite referral at discharge
New triple inhaler not picked up due to $95 copay; patient using old albuterol only
Prednisone taken every other day instead of daily due to insomnia side effect
No transportation arranged for pulmonology follow-up; patient no longer drives
Lives alone in second-floor walk-up with no local in-person caregiver
plan: Escalate DME order for portable oxygen tanks with 24-48 hour target delivery and confirm via follow-up call
Submit urgent re-referral to home health agency citing missed 48-hour contact window
Refer to pharmacy financial assistance/manufacturer copay program and screen for Medicare Extra Help (Part D Low-Income Subsidy)
Arrange Medicare-covered non-emergency medical transportation for pulmonology follow-up, accounting for oxygen equipment in transit
Coach patient and loop in pulmonology on correct prednisone taper adherence; do NOT independently adjust the steroid dose - communicate concern to prescriber
Review and document explicit escalation/red-flag criteria with patient and daughter (teach-back)
Schedule structured follow-up call within 24-48 hours to confirm all services actually connected (closed-loop coordination)

If any acute red flag emerges (SpO2 persistently <88%, worsening dyspnea at rest, confusion, chest pain, fever), direct patient to contact pulmonology urgently or call 911; this is outside case manager scope to manage directly
redFlags: SpO2 sustained below prescribed target range off oxygen or not improving with oxygen
Increasing respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, or inability to speak full sentences
New fever, chest pain, or change in sputum color/volume
Any of the above warrants direct escalation to pulmonology or emergency services, not management by case management alone
educationPoints: A 'fine, baby' opening answer in a patient with repeat admissions warrants structured, specific barrier screening before accepting it at face value
Cost-related non-adherence is common and often hidden; direct, non-judgmental questions about copays and affordability should be routine
Medication side effects (like insomnia from prednisone) can drive silent self-rationing that looks like noncompliance but is symptom avoidance
Discharge plans with multiple vendors (DME, home health, specialty clinic) require active closed-loop confirmation; orders being placed does not mean services were delivered
Transportation and mobility barriers are frequently the hidden reason for missed specialty follow-up, especially when a patient has stopped driving
Case managers coordinate and escalate; medication dose changes and clinical destabilization decisions belong to the prescribing/treating clinician

artifacts.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
artifacts.author: Dr. Patel, Hospital Medicine
artifacts.body:
76-year-old female admitted for acute exacerbation of COPD (3rd admission this calendar year). Treated with nebulized bronchodilators, IV then oral corticosteroids, and supplemental oxygen. Improved to baseline function at discharge.

Discharge medications: Trelegy Ellipta (fluticasone furoate 100mcg/umeclidinium 62.5mcg/vilanterol 25mcg) 1 inhalation daily - NEW; Prednisone taper: Days 1-3 40mg daily, Days 4-6 30mg daily, Days 7-9 20mg daily, Day 10 10mg, then stop; Albuterol HFA 90mcg 2 puffs q4-6h PRN - continue.

Home oxygen: 2L/min via nasal cannula continuous, plus portable tank/concentrator ordered for ambulation and appointments - DME referral placed.

Services ordered: Home health nursing evaluation within 48 hours of discharge for medication teaching and respiratory assessment. Pulmonology follow-up appointment scheduled in 7 days at University Pulmonary Associates.

Patient counseled on red flags: worsening shortness of breath, fever, change in sputum, chest pain, confusion - instructed to seek care immediately if these occur.

cells: Days 1-3: 40mg; Days 4-6: 30mg; Days 7-9: 20mg; Day 10: 10mg, then stop
Daily (tapering), see dose by day range

artifacts.title: Admission History - COPD Exacerbations This Year
Home Pulse Oximetry Readings Since Discharge
Pharmacy Fill History
artifacts.body: Pharmacy records show: Albuterol HFA inhaler last filled 6 weeks prior to this admission, prior to hospitalization - no new fill since discharge. Trelegy Ellipta: new prescription sent to pharmacy at discharge, status 'not picked up,' quoted patient copay $95.00 under current Part D plan tier. Prednisone 40mg #30 tablets: filled on day of discharge, quantity sufficient for full 10-day taper if taken as prescribed; pharmacy refill history shows no additional fills needed or requested, consistent with original fill still on hand.

artifacts.title: Home Health Referral Status
artifacts.body: Referral for home health nursing evaluation submitted electronically on discharge date to Riverside Home Health. Status in referral tracking system: 'Received - pending scheduling.' No documented patient contact or visit note on file as of today, day 4 post-discharge. Agency's standard contact window is within 48 hours of referral receipt.

artifacts.title: DME (Durable Medical Equipment) Order Status
artifacts.body: Order for stationary oxygen concentrator (2L/min) marked 'Delivered' on discharge day. Separate order for portable oxygen tanks/portable concentrator for ambulation marked 'Order placed, awaiting fulfillment' - no delivery date confirmed in vendor system as of today.

facts.chart: Patient contacted for scheduled post-discharge transition-of-care call following recent COPD exacerbation hospitalization.
facts.says: Oh, hi honey, I figured the hospital would check in. I'm doing fine, really, no need to worry about me.

facts.chart: Patient confirms recent 5-day hospitalization for COPD exacerbation, third this year.
facts.says: Yes, I was in there about a week, this is the third time this year it's happened, seems like.

facts.chart: Patient reports breathing is 'about the same' as at discharge, denies acute worsening.
facts.says: My breathing's about the same as when I left the hospital. Not worse, just still kind of winded.

facts.chart: New triple-combination inhaler not picked up from pharmacy due to cost barrier.
facts.says: That new inhaler, the fancy one, I went to pick it up but they said it was going to be ninety-five dollars and I just... I put it back. I'm still using my old one.

facts.chart: Continues using prior albuterol HFA inhaler as sole respiratory medication.
facts.says: I've just been using my regular puffer, the blue one, like I always have.

facts.chart: Reports taking prednisone every other day rather than daily taper as prescribed.
facts.says: That steroid pill, I take it, but not every single day. It keeps me up all night and I can't take that on top of everything else.

facts.chart: Stationary oxygen concentrator present and in use at 2L/min; no portable tanks delivered.
facts.says: They brought the big machine for the apartment, that part's here and running. But the little tanks for going out, those never came.

facts.chart: Has not left apartment since discharge due to lack of portable oxygen.
facts.says: I haven't been outside since I got home. Can't carry that big machine down the stairs, and the little tanks never showed up.

facts.chart: No contact from home health nursing agency since discharge, 4 days prior.
facts.says: Nobody's called me from any home nurse people. I've just been waiting.

facts.chart: No transportation arranged for upcoming pulmonology follow-up; patient no longer drives.
facts.says: That lung doctor appointment is clear on the other side of town. I don't drive anymore, haven't for a couple years, so I don't know how I'm getting there.

facts.chart: Lives alone in a second-floor walk-up apartment with no elevator.
facts.says: I'm up on the second floor, no elevator, just the stairs. Been living here about fifteen years.

facts.chart: Daughter lives in Texas, calls daily by phone; cannot provide in-person caregiving.
facts.says: My daughter calls me every single day, bless her heart, all the way from Texas. She worries so much.

facts.chart: Patient initially minimizes difficulties, states she doesn't want to be a burden to her daughter or care team.
facts.says: I don't like to make a fuss. My daughter's got her own life out there, I don't want her worrying more than she already does.

facts.chart: Has traditional Medicare with a Part D drug plan; no Extra Help/Low-Income Subsidy or additional supplemental drug assistance on file.
facts.says: I've got my Medicare, that's it. Never signed up for any extra help with the drug costs, didn't know there was such a thing maybe.

facts.chart: Fixed income from Social Security after retiring from cafeteria work; limited discretionary funds for unexpected copays.
facts.says: I'm retired now, just get my Social Security check. Ninety-five dollars extra just isn't sitting around waiting to be spent.

facts.chart: Denies fever or chills.
facts.says: No fever, no chills, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Denies chest pain.
facts.says: No pain in my chest, no.

facts.chart: Denies change in sputum color or amount; describes it as usual whitish/clear.
facts.says: What I cough up looks the same as always, kind of whitish.

facts.chart: No confusion; oriented and conversant throughout the call.
facts.says: My head's clear, I know what day it is and everything.

facts.chart: Denies new leg swelling.
facts.says: My legs look the same, no extra swelling that I can see.

facts.chart: Reports adequate groceries for about one week via neighbor assistance; no acute food insecurity.
facts.says: A neighbor got me some groceries, I've got enough for about a week, I think.

facts.chart: No grab bars installed in bathroom; patient has not fallen but reports feeling unsteady at times.
facts.says: No bars in the bathroom, no. I do feel a little unsteady sometimes getting up but I haven't fallen.

facts.chart: States she understands the prednisone taper was supposed to decrease every few days but has not been following the schedule as written.
facts.says: I know it's supposed to go down a little every few days, that's what they told me, but I just take it when I feel like I can handle not sleeping.

facts.chart: Expresses frustration about repeated hospitalizations and feeling like the plan set up for her does not work in her real life.
facts.says: Three times this year, baby. I keep going in, they fix me up, send me home with a plan, and the plan just doesn't fit how I actually live.

facts.chart: Pulmonology office has not called to confirm or remind about the follow-up appointment; patient only has date written on discharge paperwork.
facts.says: Nobody from the lung doctor's office has called. I just have the date written on that paper they gave me.

facts.chart: History of hypertension, controlled, and osteoarthritis affecting knees, contributing to mobility limitation on stairs.
facts.says: I've got my blood pressure pills too, and my knees give me trouble, arthritis they call it.

facts.chart: Retired cafeteria worker, worked in school food service for over 30 years before retiring.
facts.says: I worked in the school cafeteria for over thirty years, feeding all those children. Loved that job.

facts.chart: Reports taking lisinopril for blood pressure regularly as prescribed, no issues.
facts.says: My blood pressure pill, I take that one every morning, no trouble with that one at all.

facts.chart: Initially guarded and minimizes problems; opens up more once rapport is established and she senses non-judgmental listening.
facts.says: You're not going to put me back in that hospital for telling you all this, are you?

facts.chart: Spends most of day in recliner near window; reports feeling isolated and bored being homebound since discharge.
facts.says: I just sit in my chair by the window most of the day. Gets lonely, not being able to get out at all.

facts.chart: Former smoker, quit approximately 10 years ago, no current tobacco use.
facts.says: I used to smoke but I quit that about ten years back, haven't touched one since.

facts.chart: States her main goal is to stay out of the hospital and be able to see her daughter when she visits next month.
facts.says: I just want to stay out of that hospital, and my daughter's coming to visit next month, I want to be up and able to enjoy it with her.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she takes the prednisone but not every day because it disrupts her sleep.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy fill history shows prednisone #30 tablets filled on discharge day in a quantity sufficient for the full prescribed 10-day taper, with no additional refill requested - consistent with the original fill still largely on hand, supporting that she has not been taking it as prescribed daily.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Pharmacy fill/refill patterns can help a case manager objectively corroborate (or gently probe) a patient's self-reported adherence without being confrontational; the goal is understanding the barrier (insomnia side effect), not catching the patient out.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states no one from home health has called her at all since discharge.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Home health referral status shows the referral was received by Riverside Home Health and is 'pending scheduling' with no documented contact - confirming the patient's report and revealing the agency missed its own 48-hour contact standard.
mismatches.teachingPoint: This is a confirming mismatch rather than a contradiction: cross-checking the patient's report against the referral tracking system validates the gap and gives the case manager concrete evidence to escalate with the agency rather than relying on secondhand recollection alone.

objectives.text: Elicit medication adherence barriers related to cost and side effects despite initial minimization, distinguishing cost non-adherence from clinical refusal.
Identify breakdowns in the discharge plan across multiple domains: oxygen equipment, home health follow-up, and transportation.
Perform a remote respiratory status check and screen for red-flag symptoms to determine whether the situation requires urgent escalation versus care coordination.
Recognize and respectfully probe a patient-chart mismatch regarding home health contact and medication adherence using existing record evidence rather than confrontation.

Prioritize and arrange appropriate services (expedited DME, home health re-referral, pharmacy assistance, transportation) within case management scope, deferring medication dosing decisions to the prescribing clinician.
Establish clear, teach-back confirmed escalation triggers with the patient and her out-of-state daughter for safety netting.

patient.name: Bernice Holloway
patient.appearance: An older woman with gray-streaked hair pulled back, seated in a worn recliner near a window with daylight coming in. She wears a floral housedress and has a nasal cannula visible, tubing running off-screen to an oxygen concentrator; her affect is pleasant and a little guarded at first, with occasional pauses to catch her breath mid-sentence.

persona.personality: Warm, proud, and used to taking care of others rather than being taken care of. Polite and a bit guarded about admitting trouble, with a dry sense of humor once she relaxes.
persona.communicationStyle: Calls people 'baby' or 'honey' affectionately, speaks in full unhurried sentences, tends to downplay problems with phrases like 'I'm fine' before slowly revealing details once trust builds.
persona.emotionalState: Tired and a little discouraged under a composed surface; worried about being seen as a burden or about being sent back to the hospital for being honest.
persona.background: Worked in a school cafeteria for over 30 years before retiring, raised her daughter mostly as a single parent, has lived in the same second-floor apartment in St. Louis for 15 years. Enjoys watching game shows and keeping up with her church group by phone. Her daughter moved to Texas for work years ago and calls every day.
speechExamples: Oh, I'm fine, baby, don't you worry about me.
Three times this year now, seems like I just can't catch a break.
That medicine, the new one, they wanted ninety-five dollars for it, if you can believe that.
I don't like to make a fuss, my daughter's got enough on her plate.
You're not going to send me right back to that hospital for telling you this, are you?
concerns: Being readmitted to the hospital again
Being a burden to her daughter
Losing independence and not being able to manage stairs or get outside
Affording her medications on a fixed income
Missing her daughter's upcoming visit if she is not doing better

scenario.studentBrief: You are a nurse case manager making a routine telephone/video transition-of-care call to Bernice Holloway, 76, four days after discharge from her third hospitalization this year for a COPD exacerbation. Review the discharge plan, assess how the transition is actually going, identify any gaps or barriers, and coordinate next steps within your scope as a case manager.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Post-discharge follow-up after COPD exacerbation hospitalization
scenario.openingLine: Oh, hi honey, I figured the hospital would check in. I'm doing fine, really, no need to worry about me.
tasks: Review the discharge plan and reconcile it against what is actually happening at home (medications, oxygen, home health, follow-up appointment)
Build rapport to uncover barriers the patient is initially reluctant to share (cost, side effects, transportation, isolation)
Perform a basic remote respiratory status check and screen for red-flag symptoms requiring urgent escalation
Prioritize and arrange services to close identified gaps (expedited portable oxygen, home health re-referral, pharmacy financial assistance, transportation)
Document a case management assessment and care plan, and set clear escalation triggers with the patient and her daughter

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in her second-floor walk-up apartment in St. Louis, Missouri
profile.summary: A 76-year-old woman with recurrent COPD exacerbations (third hospitalization this year) is called four days post-discharge for a routine transition-of-care check-in, and initially insists she is 'fine' before a skilled case manager uncovers that nearly every element of her discharge plan has quietly failed: no portable oxygen, an unaffordable new inhaler, no home health contact, no transportation to follow-up, and self-rationed prednisone due to insomnia. The case teaches learners to move past surface reassurance to identify layered access barriers, perform a basic remote safety screen, and coordinate services within case management scope while appropriately deferring medication and clinical decisions to the prescribing team.
profile.title: Unraveling a Silent Readmission Risk: Post-COPD Discharge Transition Call
